name: Traditional PKI vs DLT
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Certificate Authorities and Ledgers: Two Answers to Who Do You Trust
lesson.summary: Traditional public key infrastructure and distributed ledger technology both try to let strangers verify identity and authenticity cryptographically, but they place trust in different places, a small set of certificate authorities versus a distributed network, and real deployments show each approach still has a distinct role.
lesson.body:
This closing chapter compares two answers to a question that has run through this entire section: when a system needs to verify that something is authentic, where should trust actually live? It builds directly on public key infrastructure and distributed ledger technology, so it is worth recapping each briefly before comparing them.

Traditional public key infrastructure, PKI, relies on certificate authorities, organizations trusted to issue and vouch for digital certificates that bind a public key to a specific identity, most commonly a website's domain name. Your browser trusts a website's certificate because it trusts the certificate authority that signed it, and certificate authorities sit in a hierarchy rooted in a relatively small number of root certificates that come pre-installed in operating systems and browsers. A distributed ledger takes a different approach to the same general problem: instead of concentrating trust in a small set of designated authorities, many independent participants maintain and agree on a shared, append-only record through a consensus protocol, so no single party, or small group of parties, is the sole gatekeeper of what counts as true.

Comparing the two directly on the problem they are both used to solve, proving something is authentic and has not been secretly altered, is where the tradeoffs become concrete. Traditional PKI's historical weak point is the certificate authority itself. If a certificate authority is compromised, or issues a fraudulent certificate, the entire chain of trust rooted in that authority breaks; this is not hypothetical, the 2011 compromise of the certificate authority DigiNotar led browser makers to stop trusting its certificates entirely, and revocation, the process of telling every client "stop trusting this certificate," has historically been slow and unreliable, since older mechanisms like certificate revocation lists and OCSP have known gaps. Certificate Transparency, a system built by Google, was created specifically to catch this kind of certificate authority misbehavior faster: it requires certificate authorities to publish every certificate they issue into public, append-only logs built on Merkle tree hash chaining, so anyone can audit what has been issued and detect a fraudulent certificate quickly. It is worth pausing on Certificate Transparency as a genuinely useful real-world system that borrows blockchain-like ideas, cryptographic hash chaining, public append-only logs, without actually being a blockchain: there is no cryptocurrency, no proof-of-work or proof-of-stake mining, and no decentralized consensus among unrelated validators. It is one well-designed piece of cryptographic engineering solving a specific, real problem, and a good reminder that not every tamper-evident system needs to be a full blockchain to be effective.

On the distributed ledger side, projects pursuing what is often called self-sovereign identity, such as the Sovrin Network built on Hyperledger Indy, have tried to let a person hold their own verifiable credentials and prove specific claims about themselves without needing a central authority to vouch for them at the exact moment of verification. Despite years of development, this approach has not reached anything close to the mainstream adoption that traditional PKI has, which quietly secures the overwhelming majority of everyday web traffic through TLS.

The honest conclusion, tying together this entire section, is that neither approach has fully solved the underlying problem; each has made a different, defensible tradeoff about where trust has to live. Traditional PKI's centralization is a real weakness, a compromised or coerced certificate authority is a single point of failure, but it is fast, cheap, well understood, and already running at a scale that secures billions of daily connections. Distributed ledger based identity removes that single point of failure in principle, but it has struggled with adoption, usability, and the very same governance questions, who decides which network is authoritative, how a compromised credential actually gets revoked, that came up repeatedly throughout the earlier case studies in this section. As with almost everything else covered here, the right takeaway is not that one approach has won, but that each makes an honest, specific tradeoff, and the skill worth keeping from this whole section is asking which tradeoff a given problem actually needs.
